newsitem.title: JAPAN: Number of big bankruptcies jumps in Japan.
newsitem.headline: Number of big bankruptcies jumps in Japan.

text.p: The wave of corporate bankruptcies in Japan swept up a larger number of big firms in February that were swamped by a backwash of "bubble era" debts and slow economic recovery.

The number of large-scale bankruptcies -- involving debts of more than 1 billion yen ($8.1 million) -- hit 95 in February, the second-largest number ever in a single month, private research firm Tokyo Shoko Research Ltd. said Friday.
Of those, 16 firms had debts of more than 10 billion yen ($81.3 million). The record for large-scale bankruptcies in a single month is 102 in December 1991.

"Corporate bankruptcies rose for the second consecutive month (year-on-year) as failures of fairly large companies caused by severe business conditions are increasing..." Tokyo Shoko said in a report.
The companies are still dealing with the aftermath of the early 1990s bursting of Japan's "bubble economy" of inflated land and stock prices.

Among the major casualties in February, hotel operator Gajoen Kanko KK failed with debts totalling 15.4 billion yen ($125 million). Gajoen Kanko was listed on the first section of the Tokyo Stock Exchange.

In terms of debt, the biggest bankruptcies were Marutaka KK, an Osaka-based real estate developer, with debts of 62.3 billion yen ($506 million), and leading women's wear retailer Suzuya, with debts of 58.7 billion yen ($477 million), the report said.

Tokyo Shoko said the total debts held by companies that went under in February fell 17.5 percent from the same month last year to 743.6 billion yen ($6.04 billion), but the figure was up 10.3 percent from January.
The total number of bankruptcies in February increased 5.2 percent from a year earlier to 1,225, the report said, but was down 0.8 percent from January.
It did not explain why total debt fell while the number of bankruptcies increased.

The report said about 56 percent of the bankruptcies were due to factors typical in a slow economy. It said 536 failures were caused by sluggish sales, while 122 firms went under because of accumulated losses.

Bankruptcies in the construction sector rose 13.4 percent year-on-year to 356 firms, while failures in the manufacturing sector rose 13.1 percent to 241. Failures in the real estate sector decreased 4.3 percent from a year earlier to 44, while those in the financial sector declined 28.6 percent to five, the report said.
There was a total of 11,448 employees at the firms that went under, it said.
